title: The colors
hookLine: sunsets redden because light crosses more air and the blues scatter away

cards: At noon, the sky is blue and the sun is a hard white. In the last hour before dark, everything goes gold.
Then orange, then pink, sometimes a red so deep it looks painted, and after the sun is gone, a soft blue-violet that seems to glow from nowhere. Same sun. Same sky.
Same air. So where do the colors come from, and why only now? A child might ask it.
Scientists asked it too, and the answer took them until the eighteen hundreds.

teach.b: Sunlight looks white, but it's every color mixed together, as a rainbow shows. Passing through the air, it bumps into molecules far too small to see, and they scatter some of it in every direction.
The key: they scatter the short, blue wavelengths much more than the long, red ones.
In the eighteen sixties the Irish physicist John Tyndall studied this in the lab, and in 1871 the English physicist Lord Rayleigh worked out the math. It's called Rayleigh scattering.
At noon, the sun is high, and its light takes a short path through the air.
Blue gets scattered all over the sky, which is why the sky looks blue. At sunset, the sun is low, and its light slants through many times as much air to reach you.

teach.h: A LONG ROAD THROUGH THE AIR.
teach.b: Along that long road, most of the blue is scattered off to the side. What arrives at your eyes is the long-wave light: yellow, orange, red. Dust, smoke and tiny droplets can deepen it.

After the volcano Krakatoa erupted in 1883, its ash and gases spread high around the world, and people as far away as Europe and North America saw sunsets so fiery that some thought there was a fire in the distance.
And after the sun disappears, clouds high up can still catch its light, blushing pink while the ground goes gray. Knowing the physics takes nothing from the view.
Tonight's orange is sunlight that slanted through a long road of air, and lost its blue on the way to you.

how: Painters, photographers and sky watchers study sunset colors closely, and physics classes explain them with Rayleigh scattering: blue light scatters more, so a low sun looks orange and red.

o: the sun's light itself turning red as it sets
the sun cooling down as evening comes on
the reds left when the low sun's blues scatter away

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.

s: at sunset, the sun's light itself changes color
the sun is the same; its light crosses more air, and the blues scatter away.
air scatters blue light more than red
that's Rayleigh scattering, and it's why the daytime sky is blue.
after Krakatoa, some people thought distant fires were burning
the ash made sunsets so fiery that some saw them as fire on the horizon.

games.q: the sun is low, and its light slants through far more air than at noon. what happens to the blue?
games.why: most of the blue is scattered off to the side along the long road. what reaches your eyes is yellow, orange and red.

practice: Look slowly around the room you're in and find three colors, not just blue or white but the exact shade: the gray-green of a plant, the honey of a wooden table, the pale pink of a hand. Name each one inside.
Tonight's sky can get the same close look.

wordCard.voice: The colors. Sunsets redden because the low sun's light crosses more air, and the blues scatter away. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: three colors. Same sun, same sky, a longer road of air. Day one hundred fifty, done.
